system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2152-07-27 23:47:00 to 2152-08-02 17:24:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of chronic pancreatitis and anxiety presented with acute-on-chronic abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She was managed conservatively with IV fluids, pain control, and anti-nausea medications. Her symptoms improved rapidly, allowing advancement to a soft diet and transition to oral medications. She remained pain-free by discharge, was ambulatory, and expressed readiness to return home. She was discharged with instructions to slowly advance her diet, avoid alcohol, and monitor for recurrent symptoms, with prescriptions for prochlorperazine, acetaminophen, and continued management of her psychiatric and gastrointestinal conditions.

radiology_notes.text:
REASON FOR THE EXAMINATION:  This is a ___ woman with history of
recurrent acute pancreatitis and abdominal pain.  Has a presumptive history of
sphincter of Oddi spasm to evaluate for evidence of source of symptoms and
biliary ductal changes to support sphincter of Oddi spasm.

COMPARISON:  Previous MRCP with secretin injection from ___ and CT of the
abdomen and pelvis from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multiplanar T1- and T2-weighted images were acquired on a 1.5
Tesla magnet including dynamic 3D imaging obtained prior to, during, and after
the uneventful intravenous administration of 15 ml of Magnevist.  In addition,
300 ml GastroMARK +450 cc of Redicat were given orally.  1 mg of secretin was
injected intravenously.

FINDINGS:  A tiny liver lesion is seen on segment VII that is of increased T2
signal and show no enhancement consistent with tiny liver cyst.  Otherwise,
the liver is of normal signal.

Few foci that shows increased arterial enhancement are seen in the liver ( for
example: ___, ___ and ___, 27) that fades into liver signal on delayed
imaging and most probably represent perfusional anomalies.

The gallbladder is within normal limits.  There is no intra- or extra-biliary
duct dilatation.

The pancreatic duct is not dilated and of normal appearance before secretin
injection.  After secretin injection, there is greater than normal dilation of
the pancreatic duct, some irregularities are seen throughout the duct with the
prominent one seen in the body segment ( 14,15 ).  No filling defects are
observed. Numerous side branches are detected after secretin injection with
the prominent one seen on the head segment ( 14,17 ). Visualization of the
Santorini and the uncinate process ducts are better appreciated after secretin
injection.
Of note, the duct diameter does not go back into its baseline diameter after
10 minutes. 
There is diffuse decreased T1 weighted signal throughout the pancreas
parenchyma. 
In addition, fillinig of the duodenum is mildly delayed and might be through
the Santorini ducts. All these findings are more prominent than on previous
examination.

The spleen and adrenals are normal.

Tiny increased T2-weighted signal that shows no enhancement is seen on the
right kidney in the interpolar region.  Otherwise, both kidneys enhance and
secrete adequately.

The visualized small and large bowels are within normal limits.  There is no
lymphadenopathy or free fluid that is observed.

Osseous structures are within normal limits.

IMPRESSION:  
Greater than normal dilation of the pancreatic duct after secretin injection
which persists at 10 minutes, with main duct mild irregularity and numerous
small side branches seen. In addition, filling of the duodenum is mildly
delayed and is at least partially through the duct of Santorini. All these
findings are more prominent than on previous examination and meet the criteria
for chronic pancreatitis,which might be the result of sphincter of oddi spasm
or stenoisis at the papilla.

Diffuse decreased T1-weighted signal throughout the pancreas parenchyma in
keeping with chronic pancreatitis and new since ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I had that MRCP with secretin yesterday, and shortly after, I started having that same sharp pain in my upper belly—epigastric, like before. It’s been getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, and any nausea? Vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, nausea for sure, but I haven’t thrown up. I’ve had this before after the MRCP—last time it flared up too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Given your history of chronic pancreatitis, the secretin can sometimes trigger a flare. We’ve checked your blood work, and your lipase is elevated—662—so this does look like another episode of acute pancreatitis on top of your chronic condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, great. So it’s not just me imagining it. What happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you NPO—for now, no food or drink by mouth—to let your pancreas rest. We’ll give you IV fluids to stay hydrated and Dilaudid for pain control. You’ll also get medication for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I remember Zofran usually helps, but I’m allergic to that, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re allergic to Zofran. We’ve given you Phenergan initially and will switch to Reglan, which should help with nausea without the risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my anxiety’s been worse with the pain. I take clonazepam and fluoxetine—can I keep those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued your fluoxetine, imipramine, and clonazepam. We’ll also have Ativan available if you need extra help with nausea or anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just want to get through this flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling? Pain level?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still some pain, maybe a 5 out of 10. Nausea’s a bit better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lipase this morning dropped to 100, which is a good sign—your pancreas is calming down. We’ll keep you on IV fluids and pain meds for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the MRCP results? Did they show anything new?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the scan showed more dilation of the pancreatic duct after secretin, and it didn’t return to normal after 10 minutes. There’s also irregularity in the duct and more side branches—signs of chronic pancreatitis. It also suggests possible sphincter of Oddi dysfunction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I keep flaring after the test? Is there a fix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a contributing factor. GI has been consulted. They recommend treating the acute flare now and planning an outpatient EUS—endoscopic ultrasound—to get a better look. They’ll contact you to schedule it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds like a plan. I just hope we can figure this out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re going to try advancing your diet today—start with clear liquids. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, maybe a 3 now. I’m nervous about eating—last time it made it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We’ll go slow—clear liquids first, and if you tolerate it, we’ll move to soft foods tomorrow. We’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try. Any updates on my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve kept your psychiatric meds running. Your ranitidine and nitroglycerin SR are also continuing. We’re watching for any side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well on clear liquids. We’re upgrading to a soft diet today—mashed potatoes, applesauce, things like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m hungry. But should I avoid anything specific?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—avoid fatty foods, alcohol, and large meals. Stick to small, low-fat portions. We’ll give you written instructions before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And what about pain meds when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with Dilaudid for breakthrough pain—take it only as needed. Also Reglan for nausea and Ativan if nausea or anxiety flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been pain-free since yesterday and are tolerating the soft diet well. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. Will I need another hospital stay like this again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope not. The key is managing triggers—avoiding alcohol, eating small low-fat meals, and following up with GI. The EUS might help us decide if there’s a structural issue we can fix.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my anxiety? It really spikes during these flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve adjusted your fluoxetine to 20 mg daily—lower dose for now. Continue your clonazepam and imipramine. Talk to your psychiatrist if anxiety remains hard to manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I will. Thank you for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final day in the hospital. You’re still doing well—no pain, eating without issues. We’ll finalize your discharge plan today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. What meds am I taking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take fluoxetine 20 mg daily, ranitidine 150 mg twice daily, clonazepam 1 mg at bedtime, and imipramine 10 mg daily. Prazosin twice daily, and trazodone as needed for sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the nitroglycerin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one 2.5 mg extended-release capsule at bedtime. It’s still being used to help with possible sphincter of Oddi spasm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And Zyrtec at night too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one capsule at bedtime for your seasonal allergies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a lot, but I think I can manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your condition is stable—pain-free, eating well, and ambulatory.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Any final instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Continue the soft, low-fat diet and advance slowly. Avoid alcohol completely. Take your meds as prescribed. Watch for worsening pain, fever, or vomiting—return if those happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up with GI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. GI will call you to schedule the EUS. They’ll evaluate whether you might benefit from further intervention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I really appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in before you leave—any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got everything. The nurse reviewed the meds and diet. I feel ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember, call your doctor or come back if symptoms return. Take it easy at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. You’re officially discharged. Transportation is on the way?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my sister’s picking me up. I’m so glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. Keep up the progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick call to check in—how are you feeling at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I had some broth and toast, no pain. Resting now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Keep it slow. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Dr. Lee? I just wanted to say thanks again. I feel like I finally have a plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. You’re on the right track. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final follow-up call. You’re doing well, and we’re closing the admission. Rest and follow up with GI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you for everything.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of chronic pancreatitis, anxiety, and probable sphincter of Oddi dysfunction was admitted with epigastric pain and nausea following an MRCP with secretin, which triggered an acute flare of pancreatitis. She was managed conservatively with NPO status, IV fluids, Dilaudid for pain, and Reglan for nausea, avoiding Zofran due to allergy. Her lipase levels improved, and she gradually advanced to a soft diet without complications. MRCP findings confirmed chronic pancreatitis and possible sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, prompting GI consultation and plans for outpatient EUS. Her psychiatric medications were continued, with adjustments to fluoxetine. She remained pain-free, ambulatory, and mentally clear, and was discharged home with a low-fat diet plan, pain and nausea medications, and follow-up arranged with gastroenterology.
